transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-04
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~1h7m
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Ethan Brooks (Southwind, Lead ML Eng), Priya Nair (SRE), Carlos Mendes (CTO)
-- Optional summary: quick simulation review + design for token-affinity based prefetching to reduce paging and handle thundering prefixes

[00:00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving time. quick context, yes? um, we ran the small sim you sent last week and wanted to walk through patterns and a proposed plan for token-affinity prefetching.

[00:00:22] Ethan: thanks, Jordan. yeah, the sim showed a lot more spillover than we expected once sessions hit ~12k tokens. like, we started seeing K V cache evictions and then a lot of paging back to disk which spiked tail latency.

[00:00:40] Maya: mhm, that aligns with what we saw in the traces. the hot-prefixes were only a handful of session IDs but they were causing slab contention. we noticed prefetch window was too narrow so when a request came in the prefix wasn't in memory and the runtime paged.

[00:01:05] Priya: am i right that the current staging config is default ttl=30m and prefetch lookback 2 tokens? we probably need to tune that. also, our V P C setup has limited io throughput on the file-backed store, which made paging worse.

[00:01:26] Maya: yeah, and just to call out, in the traces some of the product strings are a bit munged, it looks like "Red Wood private" in the auto transcript, uh, so ignore that.

[00:01:36] Carlos: can you explain token-affinity again? i got the high-level but how does it reduce evictions without blowing memory?

[00:01:45] Jordan: sure. simple idea: instead of treating prefixes purely by recency, we bias placement and prefetch decisions by token-affinity — basically "session vectors" that indicate likely future tokens or request patterns. if a session historically produces long continuations, we keep its prefix warmer and prefetch the next N token blocks on request arrival, but we also shrink metadata for cold sessions.

[00:02:18] Ethan: right, like keep hot sessions pinned to a hot slab with hysteresis so they don't oscillate on edge bursts. we added a bloom filter in the sim to detect returning prefixes and that cut re-fetches by ~28% in the small run.

[00:02:38] Maya: we also experimented with a two-tier slab allocator: small prefixes go into L1 fast slab, large long-context prefixes are in L2 with more aggressive compression (quantization on the token embeddings cached). the tradeoff there is CPU for dequantization versus memory saved.

[00:03:05] Priya: and how aggressive is that quantization? we worry about numerical drift and hallucinations if embeddings are quantized too low.

[00:03:15] Maya: in PROTO sims we used int8 for embedding caches and int4 for older context blocks; we saw ~30% memory reduction for older blocks and negligible throughput impact on infer (because dequant is pipelined). but i flagged it as a risk for degenerate prompts — needs evals.

[00:03:40] Jordan: ok, so the immediate operational knobs we propose: increase prefix TTL for identified hot sessions, implement token-affinity scoring to bias prefetch, and add a small L1 per-GPU slab to hold the top 200 hot prefixes.

[00:03:58] Carlos: what about paging backpressure? the file store was the problem in our on-prem rack model — io saturated and the pipeline backed up raising token latency above our SLO.

[00:04:10] Maya: for on-prem/V P C cases, we recommend two mitigations: 1) async background prefetch with throttling tied to disk queue depth so we don't overwhelm IO, and 2) evict to a fast NVMe cache before cold disk. basically a spillover hierarchy: RAM -> local NVMe -> network store.

[00:04:36] Ethan: sounds good. can you also elaborate on the telemetry we need to make decisions? the sim logs were useful but not sufficient.

[00:04:46] Jordan: yes. telemetry we found critical: per-prefix hit-rate, eviction_count, last_access_ms, slab_id, slab_pressure_pct, disk_io_latency_p95, prefetch_success_rate, and a token-affinity_score. we recommend adding a prefix age histogram and request inter-arrival time distribution by prefix.

[00:05:10] Maya: and traces — trace sampling per 1k requests with KV-level events (prefetch started, prefetch hit, eviction, spill, rehydrate) was invaluable. also include the batch size that triggered the prefetched block.

[00:05:27] Priya: any heuristics for prefetch size? large prefetch reduces misses but increases mem churn.

[00:05:34] Maya: yes. we use adaptive windowing: start with a small N tokens (e.g., 128 tokens blocks) and increase multiplicatively on repeated hits up to a cap (say 2048 tokens) while watching slab_pressure_pct. if pressure crosses 70% we throttle prefetch expansion.

[00:05:58] Ethan: in our run we saw a thundering prefix — dozens of simultaneous requests for a very popular session after a marketing email — how do you prevent prefetch storms?

[00:06:10] Jordan: couple approaches. first, coordinated singleflight per-prefix: only one prefetch inflight per prefix; others wait or use degraded model fallback. second, backpressure token — if prefetch queue for that prefix > 1, route some traffic to a read-through policy that fetches on-demand but with higher latency budget. third, coat-tail caching: if you detect a prefix storm, create short-lived clones with reduced state to serve read-only requests.

[00:06:44] Carlos: read-through policy meaning what exactly?

[00:06:48] Maya: it means let the infer runtime fetch the prefix synchronously for the request (pay latency) but avoid spawning mass async prefetch jobs; combine that with sample-error budgets so we don't hit SLOs.

[00:07:02] Ethan: are these features already in Redwood runtime or are you proposing changes?

[00:07:07] Jordan: a mix. singleflight and coordinated prefetch exist in the hosted runtime but require config tuning and an additional token-affinity classifier. the NVMe layer is supported in Dedicated but needs ops guidance for customer-managed disks in Private. some of the adaptive windowing logic is prototyped in our optimizer module.

[00:07:30] Priya: about instrumentation — will we be able to tie per-prefix events to request IDs for our logs? we need chain-of-custody for audit and SLO analysis.

[00:07:39] Maya: yes, we can surface trace ids in the telemetry exports and provide a mapping table. though note, in the transcript auto-generated speaker labels are messy — i think the export attached will have structured trace IDs.

[00:07:55] Ethan: what about memory fragmentation? once we keep hot prefixes pinned, fragmentation increases and available contiguous slabs shrink.

[00:08:03] Maya: good point. we propose periodic compaction windows during low traffic; move cold small prefixes to compacted blocks and free contiguous memory. compaction frequency is an ops knob. it is CPU-costly so schedule at off-peak.

[00:08:20] Jordan: also, consider prefix coalescing — for cases where sessions share large overlapping contexts (e.g., shared system prompts), we dedupe shared segments so multiple prefixes reference same backing block and reduce duplication.

[00:08:38] Carlos: does coalescing complicate privacy or tenancy guarantees? for multi-tenant setups we must avoid cross-customer sharing.

[00:08:46] Maya: yes, we only coalesce within the same tenant and after verifying no sensitive tokens are stored in the shared segment; RBAC and KMS-protected blobs can be enforced. we won't coalesce across customers.

[00:09:00] Ethan: any quick wins we can try this week?

[00:09:05] Jordan: yes — three quick experiments: 1) increase hot TTL to 2h for top 1% prefixes; 2) enable singleflight per-prefix in staging; 3) run simulation with NVMe spill before remote store. we'll share config snippets.

[00:09:24] Maya: and we will also share the perf spreadsheet that maps memory vs tail latency vs prefetch size; it's an easy way to reason about tradeoffs.

[00:09:33] Priya: do you have a recommended guardrail for quantization in cache? we are nervous about model quality regression.

[00:09:40] Maya: for production, start with int8 for embeddings and run targeted prompt-sets across your evals for drift; treat int4 as experimental and only for cold blocks. tie regression alerts into your evaluation harness.

[00:09:56] Ethan: regarding deployments — for Private on-prem we may need an ops playbook. can you include disk layout and suggested NVMe sizing? our racks vary.

[00:10:08] Jordan: yes, we'll include an ops appendix: recommended NVMe per-GPU ratio, queue-depth tuning for kernel, and fio profile used in sims. also include a checklist for KMS and audit log mapping.

[00:10:22] Carlos: let's talk about SLA violation fallback — if we see persistent paging impacting SLOs, what's the fallback?

[00:10:31] Maya: automatic fallback options: 1) route requests to a smaller but lower-latency model variant pinned in RAM; 2) degrade non-critical calls to summary-mode that reduces context size; 3) temporarily bump dedicated capacity if on Dedicated plan. we can set thresholds to trigger each action.

[00:10:55] Ethan: can thresholds be based on disk_io_latency_p99 or slab_pressure?

[00:11:00] Maya: yes, tie to slab_pressure_pct > 80% OR disk_io_p99 > 200ms for > 30s to trigger first fallback. exact numbers are customizable.

[00:11:12] Jordan: ok, quick aside — in the sim we found a bug where prefix last_access got updated on prefetch probes which skewed recency metrics; we recommend last_access only be updated on real client access, not internal probes.

[00:11:30] Priya: good catch. that would make hotness blip artificially.

[00:11:35] Maya: also, we noticed some transcripts spelled K V as "key vee" which is fine but telemetry needs normalized prefix ids. we recommend canonical prefix hashing (sha256-based) with small prefix salt to avoid collisions.

[00:11:52] Ethan: will enabling affinity classifier add latency to request path?

[00:11:56] Jordan: it's a tiny classifier, run async or as a fast table lookup; we can run it during auth or as part of the request planning stage so it doesn't add token-path latency. in most runs classifier cost < 1ms.

[00:12:12] Carlos: ok, what do you need from us to get started?

[00:12:17] Jordan: sample traces, current slab config (sizes/aspiration), disk topology for on-prem, and a small eval prompt set for regression checks. Ethan already volunteered to run the 24h sim.

[00:12:31] Ethan: yes i'll run it and attach storage traces.

[00:12:34] Priya: we'll need documentation for the singleflight and fallback configs so SRE can implement quickly.

[00:12:41] Maya: we'll produce a short playbook plus config snippets.

[00:12:45] Jordan: recap and next steps: Jordan to share perf spreadsheet and synthetic-load script; Maya to send prefetch config snippets and playbook; Ethan to run sim and send traces; schedule follow-up in two weeks.

[00:12:58] Carlos: sounds good. thanks all.

[00:13:02] Jordan: quick closing note: expect a separate doc on operators for NVMe sizing and recommended fio profiles.

[00:13:10] (meeting closed)

Notes about transcript quality: speaker labels and some product names are imperfect; timestamps approximate.

Attachments referenced: perf-spreadsheet.xlsx (link to be shared), synthetic-load-script.tar.gz (link to be shared), playbook-prefetch.md (link to be shared)
